analytic.title: Object-oriented Design of Real-time Systems with Stereotypes *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems have inherent complexity that makes them dificult to build. Object-oriented techniques, which have been shown to be an effective means of tackling complexity in other areas of software engineering, have some problems when applied to real-time systems design. In this paper we identify some of these problems, and describe some ways of dealing with them in an integrated framework including behavioral specifications and schedulability analysis.

'This work has been supported by CICYT, projects TAP94-0001-CP and TIC96-0614 them Reactive behavior: events and sequences of actions that the system executes in response to them. 0 Timing constraints: valid time intervals for events and reactions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems are widely used in an increasing variety of application fields, from avionics and traffic control systems to communications and home appliances. All these systems require a high level of software quality, and are subject to strict operational constraints because of safety, economical, mechanical, temporal or functional requirements. The resulting complexity makes real-time systems design a challenging activity for software engineers, and has given raise to a number of design methods specifically aimed at this category of systems (e.g. [20, 13, 8, lo]).

It is commonly accepted that design methods for realtime systems have to deal with different views of the system [ l l , 151, which together make up a design model. These views enable different aspects of real-time systems to be identified and described. Some of the most important features in the design model are : 0 Functionality: data transformations, algorithms, etc. 0 Module structure: modules and relationship between them.
0 Process structure: concurrent processes and mechanisms for synchronization and communication among

In the past, most real-time design methods have emphasized process structure and reactive behavior as the fundamental views. The current trend in other application domains, however, favours object-oriented methods [2, 17,5], which enable a better structuring for large systems and give effective support for reuse. This will expectedly result in lower development costs and better maintainability, as well as enhanced reliability through the use of well proven software components. Modern programming languages, such as Ada 95 [l], Java [9], and C++ [19], support objectorientation in a number of ways, thus enabling designs to be translated into implementations. They reflect the logical structure of the system, as described by objects, classes, and the relationships among them.

In spite of its advantages, however, object-oriented design is not widely used for real-time systems. The special requirements of these systems raise a number of problems that limit the applicability of object-oriented design principles, and especially class inheritance. As a consequence, most object-oriented methods either ignore concurrency and real-time issues [ 17,5] or deal with them in a simplistic way [2] which makes them unsuitable for critical real-time systems.

As a response to this situation, real-time object-oriented methods have been developed with the intent to conciliate object orientation with the specific requirements of realtime systems. The most widely known of these methods are ROOM [ 181, and HRT-HOOD [4].

0 ROOM gives extensive support to concurrent objects and message-based communication. However, it does not support timing constraints as required in hard-real time systems, and is thus only suitable for designing soft real-time systems.

div.head: HRT-HOOD supports timing constraints and leads to
div.p: designs with a deterministic time behavior, which can be analyzed using schedulability analysis techniques [14]. However, it lacks some important elements of other object-oriented methods, especially class inheritance.

In the rest of the paper we describe a notation, based on HRT-HOOD, which overcomes some of these drawbacks, thus extending the applicability of object-oriented design to real-time systems. The notation is based on the concept of stereotypes [ 3 ] , and is suitable for hard-real-time systems with strict time constraints.
The main differences between this notation and HRT-HOOD are: 1.
HRT-HOOD do not include resource class and subsystem class stereotypes and the sporadic classes is defined with a different semantic (a sporadic class can include more than one asynchronous method).
HRT-HOOD includes active objects, not included in the notation that will be presented. We shall additionally define rules for establishing relationships among classes of different stereotypes.
HRT-HOOD does not formalize the behavior description (the behavior of objects is represented in natural language). A notation is introduced to describe classes behavior and resources usage.

The basic elements of our notation are described in section 2. Section 3 introduces a notation for describing behavioral aspects of the model. Section 4 deals with the integration of schedulability analysis in this framework, and section 5 contains an example that illustrates the use of the notation in real-time systems.

div.head: Stereotypes for real-time systems design
div.p: In object-oriented methods, a system is designed as a collection of interacting objects, which are usually grouped into classes with similar properties. Object models usually include representations of properties of classes, relationships among these, interactions among objects and dynamic behavior. Common class relationships include aggregation, inheritance, use, association and instantiation [2].

In a real-time system, there are different kinds of objects. For example, some objects may show independent behavior, while some others may be passive in nature. We shall represent these diversity in the role of objects by means of stereotype classes. A stereotype class identifies some common characteristics for a set of classes. All classes belonging to a stereotype share a number of semantic properties, which impose some restrictions on the class behavior. Examples of such restrictions can be inheritance restrictions, synchronization constraints, implicit behavior, method protocols, etc.

Different kinds of systems have different requirements with respect to the characteristics that should be abstracted in stereotypes. We have identified a set of stereotypes that represent the most common kinds of objects that can be found in real-time systems design, as well as a set of relationships that can be defined among classes belonging to these stereotypes.

div.head: Stereotypes for real-time systems
div.p: A common set of stereotypes for real-time system design includes the following : Subsystem. A subsystem is an abstraction of a complex component, which is itself made up of lower level components of any kind.

Passive Class. Instances of passive classes can only change their state when they are requested by other objects, by means of a method or operation invocation. Passive objects do not have any internal thread of control, and their operations do not have any synchronization constraints or protocols.
Protected Class. Instances of protected classes can only change their internal state through atomic operations.

Their operations are therefore executed in mutual exclusion, and can include synchronization conditions or protocols. They represent data or other objects which are used by more than one active object', in order to avoid race conditions or data corruption.

div.head: Cyclic Classes.
div.p: A cyclic object is one that executes some action at regular time intervals. Cyclic objects have an independent thread of control, and may have operations for accessing attributes or changing their value in an asynchronous fashion. Cyclic objects are used to represent periodic behavior.

Sporadic Classes. Sporadic objects execute some action in response to an occurrence of aperiodic events. The same as cyclic objects, they have independent threads of control, and may have operations for accessing attributes. A sporadic class can define a limit on the use of resources for each response to an event instance.

Resource Classes. Resource limitations can exclude some design solutions. Data resources can be represented with protected classes, but there are other resources, like CPU, U 0 devices, or memory, that impose constraints on the system execution. These objects are not part of the software system, and their behavior cannot be arbitrarily enforced. A resource object has an associated scheduling policy, which can be used for timing analysis purposes.

Environment Classes. Additional objects which are not part of the software can be needed to understand or define the system structure or operation. These objects can be used to model sources of external events or data.

Each stereotype defines different protocols for the operations of the classes they represent. For example, passive classes have no constraints or special protocols, whereas protected classes impose mutual exclusion on their operations, and the operations of sporadic classes are executed asynchronously.

div.head: Common relationships among classes include:
div.p: Usage. The description or the implementation of class may require using other class' operations or attributes. In this case we say that the first class uses the second one.
Aggregation. Objects of one class are often built by putting together one or more objects of other classes, i.e. as aggregates of these classes.

Inheritance. A class may be defined as a specialization or subset of a more general class. In this case, the specialized class usually inherits the attributes or operations of the primitive class, which can be redefined if necessary to reflect the particularities of the new class.

Instantiation. Objects are instances of classes, more than one object can be instance of a class. Additionally, generic or template classes are often used to parameterize an abstraction for different applications or situations. Concrete classes can the be defined as instances of these with particular parameters.

Not all kinds of relationships can be defined for all kinds of classes. For example, the HRT-HOOD method forbids passive classes to use constrained methods of active (cyclic or sporadic) classes, OF to include instances of these. We follow these restrictions, except for inheritance relationships. which are not allowed in HRT-HOOD, but can be used with some restrictions in our model.

div.head: Notation
div.p: We use a graphic notation which is based on HRT-HOOD.

div.head: Inheritance Relationships
div.p: The inheritance relationship raises some problems when used in real-time systems. We now comment on some of these problems, which have been taken into account in order to choose the model notations used in this and the next section, as well as for generating the analysis models.

div.head: Polymorphic methods.
div.p: Classes within an inheritance relationship can define polymorphic methods. When a polymorphic method is used, the actual method that is executed can be chosen at run-time in different ways, depending on the inheritance and object instantiation relationships.

If an inheritance relationship is defined between passive and protected classes, and both classes define the same method, the method call can be blocked if the object is an instance of the protected class, and it will not be blocked is the object is a passive object. For instance, in figure 2, the polymorphic method call can have very different execution times, depending on the object used in the call, and schedulability analysis cannot be done in a practical way to the system. This is a serious drawback for hard real-time systems design, where a worst-case schedulability analysis is always required. Similar problems are found when there are inheritance relationships between classes of other stereotypes.

div.head: Figure 2. Inheritance Problem
div.p: Programming languages have dealt with this problem in different ways. For example, in Ada 95[1] inheritance is limited to passive objects (neither protected or task types can be extended). Java [9] takes a different approach, with no restrictions on polymorphic methods, which can be executed with or without mutual exclusion. It should be noted, however, that Java in its present form is not intended for real-time systems.

div.head: Inheritance anomaly.
div.p: Another common problem in object-oriented concurrent systems is the inheritance anomaly [16]. This problem appears when subclasses of synchronization classes are defined, and they change the superclass semantics. This can create problems in the execution of active objects, specially when polymorphism is used.

Behavior inheritance. This problem appears when a behavior model and an object model are used for the same system [ 121. Inheritance relationships can create inconsistencies between both models, because some behavior models are not defined to be used with inheritance relations.
Later, in section 4.2, some restrictions will be introduced to avoid or limitate those problems. The behavior notations is defined taking in count those problems.

div.head: Modeling system behavior
div.p: Class and object models can be used to describe the system architecture, but they are not enough for dealing with such issues as model execution or code generation. In particular, object models do not describe the relations between system inputs and outputs, or the way events are handled.

Most current object-oriented methods use some kind of functional models, together with state machines, to describe the system behavior. We build on these ideas by including some elements that are required to analyse the temporal properties of the model: Execution phases. The execution of methods and cycles of cyclic objects is decomposed into a sequence of phases, that specify the functional aspects of their behavior.

div.head: Resource utilization.
div.p: The set of resources required by each phase and their utilization parameters (CPU execution times, I/O devices, memory, etc.). The resource utilization is estimated by the designer and the analysis results can be used to choose algoritms or system structure.
Class utilization. Methods of other classes that are executed during the execution of each phase. This is required in order to complete the account of resources needed to execute a phase.

A behavioral model can then be represented as a directed graph that includes: Data flows. Describe the relation of precedence between the phases of a method or cycle, and the data generated or used during the execution of these.

div.head: Methods and Attributes. The class methods and attributes
div.p: are included in the diagrams to represent the input data sources, the output data destinations and the information that is retained between executions. The methods and cyclic classes will have two associated flows, start and end, that represent the beginning and end of the execution of methods and cycles.
Actions. An action describes an execution phase. It starts when data is available at its input flows, and it produces instances of output flows at the end.
The information included in every action description is:
Input flows. The data needed to start its execution. Output flows. The data generated during its execution.
Resources needed, quantity and duration. Methods used. Attributes. Data that can be used for the generation of output data.

Figure 3 describes the behavior of the class protectedclass included in figure 1. This kind of model can be made executable, which can be used for dynamic validation [6]. In this way, design errors can be detected early in the design phase, when they are easier to remove.

div.head: Formal model
div.p: Some model evaluations cannot be done if the components used in the model description have not formal semantics. This formalization can be done in different ways. A representation in terms of HLTPN (Hight Level Timed Petri Nets) [7] has been developed for the above described elements (classes, methods, actions, flows, relations, etc.) Each element is represented by a set of places and transitions, so that its semantics is defined by a subnet. Connecting these subnets according to the relations between elements gives a full HLTPN that models the whole system [6]. HLTPN have been used as a kernel model which is hidden from the design diagrams, as a means to give a formal executable semantics to the diagram elements, and to be able to validate models by animation techniques.
Model elements, such as methods, and their inheritance relations and protocols, are represented in terms of HLTPN.

Places and transitions represent such properties as initial conditions, inheritance and polymorphism, end of the execution, return to the caller, etc. Other places and transitions represent the periodic execution of cyclic objects, and their deadlines. The scheduling policies of resource classes (preemption, round-robin, etc.) are represented with places and transitions too. Each stereotype has its semantics formalized with the subnets that represent its elements, and the stereotype to which a class belongs defines the semantics of the class.

The behavior of the system can be simulated by executing the HLTPN that models the system. This kind of simulation can be used to animate the design models. Animation events represent typical situations, such as the beginning or end of the execution of objects, method calls, or actions, etc. The animation events are associated to some transitions used in the formal models of elements.

Models of environment classes can be used to describe execution scenarios. The description of these classes defines the system input data,as well as the distribution of aperiodic events. The results of animation, and the data contents of tokens associated to flow and method arguments can be consulted in order to validate the design models. In this way, the designer can find some kinds of design errors (deadline errors, functional and behavior errors, etc.) that otherwise would be only be detected during the implementation or testing phases of system development.

div.head: Temporal Analysis
div.p: The concurrent nature of real-time systems makes it difficult to completely validate the system requirements, especially temporal requirements. Simulations can be used to validate the system under some scenarios, but the complete validation of the system is often too complex. The proposed notation makes it possible to analyze temporal requirements employing rate-monotonic analysis (RMA) techniques [ 14.1. This kind of analysis can be used to identify deadline and other timing errors prior to implementing or running the system. It provides information on whether deadlines can be guaranteed, as well as worst case response times, for cyclic and sporadic objects. Object models and behavior models can be used to automatically produce an RMA model, which can be analyzed with some commercial tools.

An RMA model includes the system events, their responses, the description of actions that make up each response and the resources used in the actions execution. The descriptions of events, actions and resources include temporal parameters, which can be derived from the above proposed design models.
Events. Each cyclic object has an associated periodic event, the start of the cycle execution. The object description includes the deadline for cyclic activities as well.

Sporadic objects are associated to external or internal events. External events are produced by environmental objects, whereas internal events are signaled by other objects, In both cases, the response to the event must be executed within a fixed deadline. In order to be able to guarantee deadlines with a finite set of resources, it is usually assumed that there is a minimum time interval between two consecutive occurrences of any event. In RMA, this is called a bounded event arrival pattern.

Responses and actions. The behavior models define the sequence of actions that are executed in order to handle each event. Actions can use other classes and objects to define their behavior. Each action has some temporal parameters, in particular those related resource usage.
Resources. Resource, protected and sporadic class descriptions define the scheduling policy used for using the objects thereof.

All this information can be analyzed using RMA techniques, so that an assessment of the timing behaviour can be obtained. In order to get deterministic worst case behavior timing, some restrictions must be kept, however: Schedulability analysis can only be carried out for systems with limited resource usage, and it must be enforced in the model: e Cyclic, sporadic, protected, resource and environment objects that generate sporadic events must be static (they cannot be created at run-time).
The temporal parameters (period, deadlines, etc.) must be constant.
e Sporadic events must be bounded. The temporal parameters must be identified in the usage relationship,
The directed graphs included in the behavior model must be restricted as follows:
e The response of methods and cycles must be independent (they cannot share flows.)
e The graphs cannot include loops. The responses defined in the graphs must be sequential, alternative or parallel.
This restriction avoids the behavior inheritance problem described in section 2.

If two classes are included in an inheritance relationship, both must belong to the same stereotype. Inheritance between classes with different stereotypes is forbidden. This restriction avoids the problem of polymorphic methods described in section 2, each method will be handled always with the same protocol (synchronous, asynchronous, protected, noprotected, etc.).

Polymorphic methods can be analyzed with alternative responses. An action that uses a polymorphic method can be analyzed as a set of alternative responses (the alternatives depend on the number of different implementations of the method). If the responses are similar (use the same resources and the same amount of time), then analysis can be realistic, but protected resources and sporadic objects require using the resource associated to them, so the analysis in those cases cannot be realistic (the blocking times can be very different).

To avoid this problem, the actions that use protected or sporadic objects must statically identify them, i.e. the objects that are used in the action must be constant, and cannot be defined by the input flows or attributes. This restriction eliminates the use relation in a polymorphic way.

Restrictions 3 and 4 allow the static identification of resource usage; data resources (protected objects), sporadic servers (sporadic objects) and device resources (object resources) can be identified in the design model, and the behavior modeling defines the amount of time they are used.

Restrictions 1 and 2 limitates the events ocurrences and their temporal parameters, and allow the representation of behavior responses in terms of RMA responses. The four restrictions allow the automatic generation of RMA models from design models.

div.head: Example
div.p: In this section a brief example will be included. Although it is not a real example, it shows some ideas about the constructions of real-time systems design models in an object-oriented style. The example is a software system that controls the speed and fuel consumption in a car. The system polls a fuel flow sensor that gives information about the amount of fuel that is being consumed. The engine wheel sends rotation signals that are used for speed calculations.

The system polls the fuel sensor periodically, and records the rotation signals in order to produce reports that are periodically sent to the user. The hardware platform includes a CPU, and some sensors and displays. The system structure includes three subsystems: speed Sampler, f u e l Consumption Sampler and report Generator. The fuel Consumption Sampler and the speed Sampler subsystems record the fuel and speed data, and the report Generator requests the data from the other subsystems and then generates a report. The speed Sampler and the fuel Consumption Sampler can be defined as specializations of a more general class, sampler. This class represents a general sampler and has operations for getting data samples and for the sampler configuration. The wheel,

div.p: which is a source of aperiodic events, is represented by an environment class. The system CPU is represented by a resource class, and its description includes the scheduling policy. Figure 4 represents the system logical structure, which consists of six classes. At this abstraction level, the system includes five objects (one instance per class but sampler), which have been hidden to avoid confusions.

The interface of the sampler class includes methods for handling samples. These methods can be used to record samples, free recorded samples or get recorded information. One method is used to configure the sampler.

Figure 5 shows the description of sampler. It contains an object of a protected class, store. This class implements all methods but conf is. is represented. This model includes a secuence of actions to handle the calls to rotation method. This is an asynchronous method used to notify the ocurrence of wheel rotations. Two actions are defined. The first one represents the processing time needed to process the event. When it has been done, the speed will be updated making a call to the method record (its description is included in the protected class store).
The report Generator consults the information recorded and removes it from the system.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The classes used in the description of real-time systems designs have different semantics associated with them, which must be taken into account for the analysis and evaluation of design models. The stereotypes proposed enable the analysis and evaluation of real-time designs, but to do this a design model must include information about the structure and behavior of the system.

The formalization of the elements that are part of the models enables validation by simulation, and fixes the semantics of the elements. Timing (RMA) analysis can be used to check for deadline errors and verify some temporal requirements.

Some temporal properties cannot be represented with deadlines (minimum or maximum intervals between the same or different methods calls, temporal ordering of methods calls, etc.). Other techniques are needed to represent and verify these restrictions, this is a future research area for our group.
